briefing.headline: Pick the editor everyone else uses.
body: VS Code is the editor. Free, fast, the most popular among working developers by a significant margin. Cursor — the AI-first editor you'll move to later — is built directly on top of it. Every shortcut you learn here transfers to Cursor, and to every other VS Code fork you'll ever touch.

Installation is fast. What takes longer is the shortcuts becoming automatic. Don't try to memorize them. Get the tool installed, learn the Command Palette, get the integrated terminal working — the rest you'll absorb while using it.

reference.title: Essential keyboard shortcuts
reference.content:
Cmd + P              Quick file open
Cmd + Shift + P      Command Palette
Cmd + B              Toggle sidebar
Cmd + `              Toggle terminal
Cmd + /              Comment current line
Cmd + D              Select next match (multi-cursor)
Cmd + Shift + F      Search across files
Cmd + ,              Open settings

reference.title: What the Command Palette is
reference.content: Cmd + Shift + P opens a search bar that runs every command in VS Code — including ones added by extensions. If you can't remember a keyboard shortcut, type what you want here. This is the most useful single shortcut in the editor.

reference.title: Open from the terminal
reference.content:
code .              Open current directory in VS Code
code myfile.js      Open one file
code ~/projects     Open a specific folder

reference.title: Extensions worth installing
reference.content: Prettier — automatic code formatting. GitLens — see who wrote any line and when. ESLint — catches common JavaScript mistakes (install when you start writing JS). Skip everything else until you have a reason to install it.

reference.title: "command not found: code"
reference.content: You skipped the "Install the code command" step, or didn't restart your terminal after. Open the Command Palette (Cmd + Shift + P) and run Shell Command: Install 'code' command in PATH. Then close and reopen iTerm2.

completion.headline: M2 complete.
completion.body: You have a working editor with terminal, extensions, and shortcuts. Next up: M3 — Git & GitHub.

steps.title: Install VS Code
steps.body: Download from Microsoft's site. Free, no account required. Don't install anything else advertised alongside it — you don't need VS Code Insiders, the Copilot upsell, or any of the bundled extensions it suggests on first launch.
notes: Go to code.visualstudio.com and click Download for Mac
Open the downloaded .zip — Visual Studio Code appears
Drag Visual Studio Code into your Applications folder
Open it: Cmd + Space → "Visual Studio Code" → Enter
If macOS asks to confirm a downloaded app: click Open
steps.verify: VS Code is open. You see a Welcome tab.

steps.title: Install the code command
steps.body: This adds a code command to your shell. Without it, you can only open VS Code from the dock or Finder. With it, you cd into any folder and type code . — VS Code opens to that exact directory, and the integrated terminal opens to the same path. You'll do this dozens of times per week.
notes: In VS Code, press Cmd + Shift + P to open the Command Palette.
Type shell command.
Click Shell Command: Install 'code' command in PATH.
Enter your Mac password if prompted.
steps.verify: Open iTerm2 and run code --version. It prints a version number, commit hash, and architecture.
steps.trouble: If command not found: code — close and reopen iTerm2. Shell needs to reload PATH.

steps.title: Open a folder from the terminal
steps.body: The standard workflow: cd into a folder, then code . to open it. The dot means "current directory." From here on, this is how you'll launch every project — never File → Open.
steps.tryCue: Run all four. The last command opens VS Code with the new folder as the workspace.
steps.code:
cd ~
mkdir vscode-practice
cd vscode-practice
code .

commandNotes.what: Open the current directory in VS Code as a workspace.
commandNotes.when: Every time you start work on a project — cd into the repo, then code . Means you're already at the right shell location for git, npm, and the integrated terminal opens to the same path.

steps.verify: VS Code opens with vscode-practice as the project folder. The Explorer (left sidebar) shows it's empty.
whenYoullReachForThis: Starting a new project session — cd into the repo, then code .
Editing your shell config to add a tool's PATH line — code ~/.zshrc opens just that file
Opening a Claude Code project from a fresh terminal — same two-command pattern, every time
Bouncing between two repos that talk to each other — open each in its own VS Code window with code . from inside each folder

steps.title: Tour the interface
steps.body: Five regions. Most of your time lives in three: Explorer (your file tree), Editor (where you edit), and Panel (the integrated terminal). The other two — Activity Bar and Status Bar — are fast-access surfaces you'll reach for less often. Know where they are so you're not hunting for them later.
notes: Activity Bar (far left, vertical icons): switch between Explorer, Search, Source Control, Run, Extensions.
Side Bar: contents of whichever Activity Bar icon is selected — usually the Explorer (your file tree).
Editor (center): where you edit files. Multiple tabs.
Panel (bottom, hidden until needed): integrated terminal, problems, output. Toggle with Cmd + `.
Status Bar (very bottom): current branch, errors, file encoding, line and column.
steps.verify: You can identify each region. Toggle the sidebar with Cmd + B and the panel with Cmd + `.

steps.title: Use the integrated terminal
steps.body: VS Code has a terminal built in. Same zsh, same Homebrew, same PATH as iTerm2 — just inside the editor, with the cwd automatically set to your project folder. Most developers stop bouncing between apps entirely and live in here. Open it with Cmd + `.
steps.tryCue: Run all three in the integrated terminal. Watch the Explorer update in real time.

commandNotes.what: Confirms the integrated terminal opened in your project folder, not your home directory.
commandNotes.when: Sanity-checking before running an install or build command — npm install in the wrong folder is how node_modules ends up in your home directory.

commandNotes.what: Creates the file in the current directory — the same directory VS Code has open as a workspace.
commandNotes.when: Confirming the terminal and the Explorer are pointing at the same place. If hello.js appears in the file tree, they are.

steps.verify: hello.js appears in the Explorer on the left. The terminal stays open at the bottom.
whenYoullReachForThis: Running npm install or npm run dev without leaving the editor
Committing changes with git add and git commit while your code is still open
Checking Claude Code's terminal output alongside the file it just edited
Running a one-off script and immediately seeing the file it produced in the Explorer

steps.title: Command Palette
steps.body: Cmd + Shift + P. The single most useful keystroke in VS Code. Every command — built-in or from extensions — is searchable here by name. When you can't remember a shortcut, you don't have to. Type what you want.
notes: Press Cmd + Shift + P.
Type "format" — see all formatting commands.
Press Escape.
Press Cmd + Shift + P again, type "theme", select Color Theme, pick one. Try Default Dark Modern or a Light variant.
steps.verify: VS Code's color theme has changed.
whenYoullReachForThis: You half-remember a feature name but not the shortcut — "split editor," "close other tabs," "reload window"
An extension's docs say "run command X" — the Command Palette is where X lives
Changing a setting you don't want to dig through the Settings UI for — Preferences: Open Settings (JSON)
Reloading the editor after an extension install acts weird — Developer: Reload Window

steps.title: Quick file open
steps.body: Cmd + P opens any file in the project by name. Fuzzy-matched — a few letters is enough. Once a project gets bigger than a handful of files, this replaces clicking through the Explorer entirely.
notes: Press Cmd + P.
Type hello.
Press Enter to open hello.js.
whenYoullReachForThis: Jumping straight to a file you know exists but don't want to navigate to — Cmd + P, a few letters, Enter
Editing a file deep in a nested folder you don't want to click through — src/components/auth/LoginForm.jsx is three letters away
Switching between two files you're editing alongside each other — Cmd + P beats clicking tabs
Re-opening a file you just closed — VS Code shows recent files at the top of the Cmd + P list

steps.title: Multi-cursor
steps.body: Edit multiple places at once. Cmd + D selects the next occurrence of whatever you've highlighted — keep pressing to add more selections. Type once and the change happens everywhere simultaneously. The first time you use this on something repetitive you'd otherwise edit one line at a time, you'll feel the time you've been wasting.
notes: Open hello.js.

Type these three lines:
let foo = 1;
let foo = 2;
let foo = 3;
Double-click one of the foos to select it.
Press Cmd + D twice — the next two foos are also selected.
Type bar — all three change at once.
Press Escape to exit multi-cursor.
steps.verify: All three lines now say let bar = N;.
whenYoullReachForThis: Renaming a variable used in three or four places when full refactor tooling is overkill
Fixing the same typo repeated through a file — select once, Cmd + D through, type the fix
Adding a prefix or suffix to a list of identifiers — select each, then type at the start or end of every selection
Converting a vertical list of values into a comma-separated line — multi-cursor at the end of each line, then type a comma

steps.title: Search across files
steps.body: Cmd + Shift + F searches every file in the project at once. Different from Cmd + F, which only searches the file you're looking at. This is how you find every place that uses a function, variable, or magic string in a codebase you don't fully know yet.
notes: Press Cmd + Shift + F.
Type bar.
Click a result to jump to it.
steps.verify: The search panel shows matches with file names. Clicking a match jumps you to the exact line.
whenYoullReachForThis: Tracking down every call site of a function you're about to change
Finding which file defines a constant or string you saw in the UI — search for the literal text
Locating a TODO comment you wrote yesterday and forgot where
Verifying you actually deleted every reference to a thing — Cmd + Shift + F the old name, expect zero results

steps.title: Install essential extensions
steps.body: Extensions add features VS Code doesn't ship with. The two below are nearly universal — most working developers run both. Skip the rest until you have a concrete reason to install one. The extension marketplace will happily try to sell you twenty more; ignore it.
notes: Click the Extensions icon in the Activity Bar (square with one block detached) — or press Cmd + Shift + X.
Search Prettier - Code formatter. Install the one by Prettier.
Search GitLens. Install the one by GitKraken.
Restart VS Code if prompted.
steps.verify: Both extensions show "Uninstall" instead of "Install" — meaning they're active.
whenYoullReachForThis: Starting a new project — install Prettier and GitLens first, before anything else
Setting up a new Mac — your extension list is one of the things to recreate
Working in a new language for the first time (Python, Go, Rust) — there's almost always an official extension that adds syntax highlighting and a language server
Picking up someone else's repo and seeing recommendations in .vscode/extensions.json — VS Code prompts you to install them

steps.title: Format on save
steps.body: Have Prettier reformat your code automatically every time you save. Stops you arguing with yourself about whitespace and quote styles — and stops you committing formatting diffs that obscure what actually changed.
notes: Open settings: Cmd + ,.
Search format on save.
Check the Editor: Format On Save box.
Search default formatter.
Set Editor: Default Formatter to Prettier - Code formatter.
steps.verify: Open hello.js, mess up the indentation, save (Cmd + S) — Prettier fixes it.
whenYoullReachForThis: Anywhere a codebase has a Prettier config — formatting becomes invisible because every save fixes it
Onboarding to a team where every file must follow shared style — format on save means you never break the rules by accident
Switching between projects with different style preferences — Prettier picks up each project's .prettierrc automatically
Stopping a Git diff from being polluted with whitespace-only changes — your local edits land in the project's canonical format

steps.title: Clean up
steps.body: Delete the practice folder. The Welcome tab is enough — no need for a leftover empty project sitting in your home directory.
steps.verify: Folder is gone. The VS Code window still showing vscode-practice now points at nothing — close it.
